title: Answers With a Source Attached
description: Ten tools that keep the source next to the claim: citation checkers, local research desks, document agents and media libraries that stay on your machine.
content:
# Answers With a Source Attached

The most expensive sentence in AI writing is the one that sounds right and cites nothing.

Legal teams found this out first — sanctions for AI-fabricated citations are now a recurring news item — but the problem is general. A confident paragraph with no provenance is worth less than a hesitant one with a page number.

The tools in this piece all treat the source as part of the product rather than an afterthought.

## Checking the claim

[[link:/tools/2261|CiteLLM]] makes every AI answer checkable. Every claim links to the exact passage in your PDF, highlighted in the original, and it works three ways: as a plugin inside ChatGPT or Claude, as a search across a document collection, and as structured extraction where every value carries a source. A reviewer approves or flags each result and the report records who approved what. Crucially, the site is explicit that a highlight shows where an answer came from, not that it is right.

[[link:/tools/2262|CiteProof]] handles the legal case specifically. It checks every citation and quoted passage in a brief against public court records before you file, including AI-fabricated citations. The free check confirms a citation exists and resolves to the case cited; a $49 Verification Record adds quote verification with the closest passage and pin cite. It also audits the other side's brief, and it publishes a false-clean ledger — zero false cleans on 17 holdout items — which is the kind of claim worth making only if you can back it.

## Reading your own material

[[link:/tools/2266|KnowNote]] is a local-first desktop workspace for reading and questioning your own documents. The embedder runs inside the app, so retrieval works offline, and every answer keeps the source passage with its place in the document recorded. No Docker, no server, no account. It is GPL-3.0, and its own documentation makes a sharp point: retrieval quality is a property of the whole pipeline, not of the vector store.

[[link:/tools/2267|ParkourNote]] takes the same instinct to everything you read. Papers, books, saved web pages, recordings and lectures go into one library; you mark a sentence and work it out in the margin, quoted text keeps its page number, and recordings get timestamps per word. Claude and ChatGPT can read the library, so the notes travel with the question.

[[link:/tools/2265|OpenDocBot]] brings your own model into Word, Excel and PowerPoint as a client-side add-in. It supports OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, DeepSeek, OpenRouter or a local Ollama endpoint, keeps document data out of any intermediate server, and offers an optional approval gate before edits land. Free for individuals and teams up to 30 users.

[[link:/tools/2263|Pen]] takes the opposite approach to control: you say what you want to understand and it researches the subject and writes the piece you will read, private until you share it. The landing page is deliberately thin, so treat it as a writing surface rather than a research desk with audit trails.

## Turning the record into prose

[[link:/tools/2264|Buildnotes]] is a skill for coding agents that reads the issues, pull requests, commits and reviews behind a feature, finds the few decisions that shaped it, draws the figures and writes it up as a post, a video or a deck. The figures are generated from the same 3D view the page shows, and the whole thing installs with one command inside the repo. It is the rare tool that makes documentation a by-product of work already done.

## The same instinct elsewhere

Three tools in other categories share the pattern of keeping the record on your machine and making it queryable.

[[link:/tools/2258|freehire]] indexes nearly five million tech jobs straight from company career boards and exposes them over MCP so an agent can search without an account. Every number on its homepage carries the endpoint behind it, which is the same discipline as a citation.

[[link:/tools/2259|Videre]] is a local-first media library: one Rust binary, one SQLite file inside the library, duplicate detection, face grouping, and search by description or example image. Nothing is uploaded, and removed files go to the Trash with one command to restore them.

[[link:/tools/2260|Scone Money]] applies provenance to your bank statement. It finds the paychecks, rent and bills in your history, projects them forward day by day, and shows the lowest point your balance will reach before it happens — a forecast you can check against the transactions it came from.

## Why provenance is the product

Every tool here answers the same objection: how do I know this is not made up?

[[link:/tools/2261|CiteLLM]] answers with a highlighted passage. [[link:/tools/2262|CiteProof]] answers with a court record and a ledger of its own mistakes. [[link:/tools/2266|KnowNote]] answers with an offline embedder and a page reference. [[link:/tools/2258|freehire]] answers with the endpoint behind the count.

That is a different value proposition from fluency, and it is the one that survives contact with a reviewer. If you write anything that someone else has to sign off on, start here rather than with the model that writes best.
tldr: CiteLLM, CiteProof, Pen, Buildnotes, OpenDocBot, KnowNote and ParkourNote make provenance part of the output, while freehire, Videre and Scone Money apply the same instinct to jobs, photos and money.
